# Design and Psychometric Evaluation of the Artificial Intelligence Acceptance and Usage in Research Creativity Scale Among Faculty Members: Insights From the Network Analysis Perspective

Ayoub Hamdan Al- Rousan[1](#design-and-psychometric-evaluation-of-the-artificial-intelligence-acceptance-and-usage-in-research-creativity-scale-among-faculty-members-insights-from-the-network-analysis-perspective)[ ](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6898-5139)\| Moha[mm](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1390-3765)ad Nayef Ayasrah[2](mailto:)[ ](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5247-2526)\| Shimaa Mkhymr Salih Yahya[3](#design-and-psychometric-evaluation-of-the-artificial-intelligence-acceptance-and-usage-in-research-creativity-scale-among-faculty-members-insights-from-the-network-analysis-perspective)[ ](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9505-5439)\| Mohamad Ahmad Saleem Khasawneh[4](#design-and-psychometric-evaluation-of-the-artificial-intelligence-acceptance-and-usage-in-research-creativity-scale-among-faculty-members-insights-from-the-network-analysis-perspective)

1Educational psychology, The Hashemite University, Queen Rania Faculty for Childhood, Early Childhood Department, Zarqa, Jordan \| 2Special Education, Al Balqa Applied University, Department of Educational Science, Irbid University College, Ibrid, Jordan \| 3Department of Educational Sciences, Irbid University College, AlBalqa Applied University, Irbid, Jordan \| 4Special Education Department, King Khalid University, Abha, Saudi Arabia

**Correspondence:** Mohammad Nayef Ayasrah ([mohammadmtlaq@bau.edu.jo)](mailto:mohammadmtlaq@bau.edu.jo) **Received:** 27 November 2024 \| **Revised:** 28 December 2024 \| **Accepted:** 5 January 2025

**Keywords:** AI adoption in academia \| artificial intelligence \| faculty members \| psychometrics \| research creativity \| technology acceptance

## ABSTRACT The acceptance of artificial intelligence (AI) in academic settings, particularly in the context of research creativity, is a growing area of interest. This study aimed to design and validate the AI Acceptance and Research Creativity Scale (AIA&RCS) among faculty members. This exploratory mixed- method was conducted among 720 faculty members. A literature review and partici- pant interviews were conducted in the qualitative phase to generate and develop items. In the quantitative phase, face validity, content validity, construct validity, convergent validity and reliability (internal consistency and stability) were used. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) indicated a 4- factor model of the scale with ‘perceived usefulness and effectiveness of AI in research cre- ativity’, ‘ethical issues in research’, ‘trusted in AI capabilities’ and ‘willingness to use AI’ accounting for 51.6% of the variance. This arrangement was verified by confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), with fit indices that were at suitable levels. Then, the net- work analysis took into account the four- factor structure of AIA&RCS further. Similarly, the exploratory graph analysis (EGA) indicated the four- factor configuration of the AIA&RCS. The 25- item scale is well- suited for measuring AI acceptance and re- search innovation among faculty because of its psychometrics.

This communication is particularly crucial in higher education, where AI technologies such as ChatGPT can transform old- school teaching and learning in a way that makes learning more personal, efficient and inclusive (Salifu et al. 2024). Technology adoption involves embracing, absorbing and employing new technologies in society, and in the higher education sector, AI and robotics are remaking the way peo- ple learn. This change is crucial for integrating contemporary teaching, as demonstrated in research on using AI robots in schools and universities, which analysed teacher and student adoption intentions (Roy et al. 2022). These data show that the more AI- driven tools educators and students embrace, the better the education and the more inclusive and effective the classroom will become (Fathahillah, Fakhri, and Ahmar  [2023;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Rahmi, Birgoren, and Aktepe 2018; Roy et al. 2022).

Creativeness—the production of valuable and new ideas—is one of the core capacities of humans. When coupled with AI, it can lead to new levels of productivity and innovation (Amabile and Pratt [2016)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for). AI creativity: using human beings and artificial in- telligence together in creative endeavours, in which they each harness their strengths to make better things happen (O'Toole and Horvát 2024; Wu et al. 2021). With a seamless connection to vast amounts of human data and analytics, AI can also comple- ment human intelligence. Technology opens the possibility for large- scale cooperation across time and space, making creativity a tool of inclusion that we had never known existed before (Wu et al. 2021). Kaufman and Beghetto's theory says that creativity comes in four levels: mini- c, little- c, pro- c and big- c creativity. These levels of creativity can be considered a continuous spec- trum, where simple, everyday activities with effort and exper- tise can evolve into creative achievements at the professional or big- C level.

By enhancing these processes, AI facilitates and expands cre- ativity at all levels (Kaufman and Beghetto 2009). As an enabling tool, AI has a great potential to enhance research creativity. By creating advanced tools, this technology enables individual, team and organisational creativity development (Perry- Smith and Mannucci  2017). This is where human–AI collaborative creativity emerged, notably to produce scientific articles and in- terpret big data. For instance, creative ideas generation tools like ChatGPT and DALL- E are generative AI models (i.e., they are used to develop creative ideas) (Ivcevic and Grandinetti 2024).

**1.1 \| AI Acceptance in Academia: Challenges and Concerns**

A setting where modern AI and related tools are widely used in academia. For example, AI tools are used to enhance learn- ing English as a foreign language (EFL) (Wang and Xue 2024; Wu, Wang, and Wang 2024) and patient information delivery (Olawade et al. 2024). Also, these uses are widely evaluated in behavioural sciences. For example, educators' perceptions of using these AI models (Huang, Wang, and Zhang 2024) and eth- ical considerations (Fangerau [2024)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) are widely discussed.

Despite the wide- ranging opportunities AI offers to research- ers, its adoption and use in academic environments face several challenges. Research indicates that various factors, including 

ethical concerns, the perceived complexity of the technology and cultural resistance, influence users' decisions to accept or reject the technology (Davis [1989;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Oliveira et al. 2024; Winecoff and Watkins 2022). For example, a common concern among fac- ulty members is the fear of reduced human interaction in educa- tional and research processes. Additionally, inadequate training and the absence of proper infrastructure are significant barriers to the widespread use of AI technologies in academic environ- ments (Guo, Shi, and Zhai 2024).

Faculty members and researchers, as the primary users of ad- vanced technologies in academic settings, play a key role in adopting and using AI. Research findings suggest that psy- chological readiness and the perceived usefulness of the tech- nology are among the determining factors in its acceptance (Alhwaiti [2023;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Ali [2023;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Falebita and Kok [2024;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Kohen- Vacs et al. 2024). While some studies indicate that faculty members in academic environments who properly recognise the added value of AI in enhancing creativity and research innovation show greater acceptance of the technology (Rana et al. 2024), AI adoption may still face challenges due to ethical concerns, limitations in technological infrastructure, complexities related to learning and usage, and cultural resistance to technological changes. These barriers are particularly evident in educational and research environments emphasising traditional methods and practices (Aithal and Maiya  [2023;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Jin et  al.  2024). This suggests that fostering a more profound and more precise un- derstanding of the benefits of AI, particularly in research cre- ativity, could improve its acceptance. However, to achieve this goal, developing a comprehensive tool to assess AI acceptance and its use in research creativity by faculty members is an es- sential research need in this field.

**1.2 \| AI Acceptance Scale: A New Perspective**

There are many scales to evaluate the acceptability of AI in differ- ent societies. Such a scale is the Generative Artificial Intelligence Acceptance Scale (GAIAS) (Yilmaz, Yilmaz, and Ceylan 2023), which measures students' tolerance for generative AI use in edu- cation. That is a key difference because faculty (though they, too, use AI tools) might have different expectations, motivations, and engagement levels than students. Thus, the scale was tailor- made for students, an audience whose AI use in schools was distinctly different. This scale, therefore, is not a good one to administer to faculty because it was not designed to evaluate how faculty perceive or act towards generative AI.

A second scale is the Teachers' Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence in Education (TAAI) scale, which assesses preser- vice teachers' acceptance of AI in the classroom (Guo, Shi, and Zhai  2024). The scale has five factors—perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioural intention, self- efficacy and anxiety. The research validating this scale involved preservice teachers in many different subjects, and the instrument is reli- able and robust, with 27 items on these dimensions. However, this scale is more focussed on teachers and their experiences in the field of AI in the classroom. Thus, it cannot be used to mea- sure faculty's acquiescence to AI because faculty regularly use AI in other, more general, nonteaching uses: research, admin- istration and decision- making. Faculty members will likely be 

interested in dimensions like AI's use for data analysis, grant submission, publication management and institutional pro- cesses, which are not addressed by the TAAI tool. Faculty might also have different anxiety or self- efficacy about AI depending on whether the AI is deployed in a high- risk research context or involves elaborate administrative operations (in contrast to the classroom- based anxieties of new faculty) (Fields, Kenny, and Mueller [2019;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Gruppen et al. 2003). Not only that but the stimuli and examples on the TAAI scale (preparation of lessons, student examinations) are distinctly taught- specific and do not extend to the various functions that faculty perform outside of teaching (Guo, Shi, and Zhai 2024).

In general, tools are in place that enable researchers to test a variety of factors impacting AI acceptance: behavioural moti- vation, mindset, perceived value, institutional infrastructure, psychological readiness and moral issues. Such dimensions can give helpful information on how users think about AI in a par- ticular environment, such as schools or workplace technology. However, for all the promise that AI might offer in terms of cre- ativity, productivity and workflow improvement, there is still no valid, standardised measure to measure AI acceptance and deployment in the academy. Current scales, whether the Student GAIAS for students or the Preservice TAAI for teachers, cannot accurately reflect faculty's particular functions and rich expe- riences with AI systems. It is common for faculty to use AI in research innovation, scholarly publication and administrative decisions—all of which require a unique assessment tool.

This will be eliminated by a scale for assessing AI acceptance among professors, allowing scientists to identify the specific barriers and facilitators to AI adoption in academia. An in- strument like this would also help extract concrete clues about what motivates faculty's perceptions of AI—from its utility to creativity in research to privacy, ethical issues and institutional support. It would also help establish successful plans for AI adoption, faculty preparation and advancing AI as widely as possible in the academic and research process. For this reason, the current research was carried out to develop and validate the ‘AI Acceptance and Research Creativity Scale (AIA&RCS)’ for faculty members. This research uses psychometric properties to develop a robust measure of AI adoption in academia.

**1.3 \| Network Analysis: A New Perspective in Psychometric Studies**

Psychometric research has generally used classic techniques such as CFA and EFA. These techniques are grounded in latent variable models, which treat constructs as unobservable things whose symptoms or indications can be measured (Davoudi, Pourshahbaz, et al. [2023;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Tosi et al. 2024). For instance, latent models could characterise COVID- 19 pathology as a condition that manifests through fever, cough and fatigue. Similarly, in psychopathology, diseases such as posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) are perceived as unrealised things that emerge as re- experiences of trauma, sleep disturbance and increased arousal.

However, new dimensional tools, like network analysis, provide a new way of thinking about psychological constructions. While latent models think of constructs as secret causes of symptoms, 

the network view considers the relationship between symptoms as the construct (Azadi et al. [2024;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Borsboom and Cramer [2013;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Davoudi, Sadoughi, et  al.  [2023;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) McNally  2021). For example, with PTSD, the network model does not consider PTSD as a sin- gle latent entity, but rather the symptoms—flashbacks, insom- nia, hypervigilance—as self- reinforcing factors, which together form the disorder. It is a method that highlights the active rela- tion of symptoms and the role of individual symptom- specificity and thus provides a richer account of complicated mental pro- cesses (Borsboom and Cramer [2013)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for).

Network analysis has gained much traction in psychometrics studies due to significant developments in its use. These are de- velopments such as the capacity to find central symptoms with the highest impact on a network and the degree of the intercon- nection between symptoms or clusters or communities within a network (Borsboom and Cramer [2013;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Davoudi et al. [2024;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Azarmehr et  al.  [2024)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for). Such knowledge can guide targeted treatments and rework theories. One promising extension of network analysis in psychometrics uses exploratory graph anal- ysis (EGA). EGA is a network approach to finding the dimen- sionality of a dataset by grouping variables into communities with a connection to each other (Abdelrahman et  al.  [2024;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Davoudi, Pourshahbaz, et al. [2023;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Golino et al. 2020; Golino and Epskamp  2017). Because EGA is free of preconceptions about the underlying structure, in contrast to other techniques, it is pretty flexible and revealing in developing and validating scales.

Hence, EGA has made it into psychometric research, and an increasing number of studies use EGA to investigate the shape and characteristics of scales. For example, this method is used in different scales such as socioemotional skills instrument for teachers (Sáez- Delgado, Mella- Norambuena, and López- Angulo  2024), life satisfaction scale (Dominguez- Vergara et al. [2024)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for), Brief Inventory of Perceived Stress (BIPS- C) (Meng et al. 2024) and Intuitive Eating Scale- 2 (IES- 2) (Ji et al. 2024). Therefore, this method of developing a psychometric estimation of the AIA&RCS could provide a dimensional perspective in the context of AI acceptance.

**1.4 \| Current Study**

The current study developed the Arabic version of the AIA&RCS. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA), EGA, and con- firmatory factor analysis (CFA) were employed to validate the scale. Additionally, convergent validity was assessed using the average variance extracted (AVE) and composite reliability (CR) criteria. Finally, the study examined the scale's internal consis- tency, with a minimum acceptable threshold of 0.70 considered for reliability.

**2 \| Theoretical Basis**

In the case of AI technologies, the accelerated growth has created new possibilities for research creativity on the part of university faculty. The design of this article takes up some major models and theories of AI acceptance and AI research innovation.

3 of 16

This is a variation of the technology acceptance model devel- oped by Davis ([1989)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for), widely adopted as a theoretical model of how users behave when using new technologies. This model identifies two important variables: Perceived Usefulness and Perceived Ease of Use (Davis  [1989)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for). The findings of various studies have demonstrated that these two factors are potent for attitudes towards technological use and have an indirect effect on intention to act (Nasser Al- Suqri 2014; Tubaishat 2018). In terms of AI acceptance, this theory can describe how faculty use AI tools for their perceived convenience and ease of use in their research projects.

Ajzen  ([1991)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) created the theory of planned behaviour (TPB) based on three elements: attitude to the behaviour, subjective norms and perceived behavioural control (Ajzen [1991)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for). For AI acceptance, faculty members' views about AI, social encourage- ment (from the institution or other faculty members) and skills with AI tools can all affect whether a faculty member uses AI for research and teaching.

UTAUT, the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (Venkatesh et al. 2003), four constructs of perfor- mance expectancy (the expectation that the technology will enhance performance), effort expectancy (ease of use of the technology), social influence (social coercion to employ the technology) and facilitating conditions (infrastructure and re- sources for the application of technology) predict behavioural intention (Venkatesh et al. 2003). The model can help account for how faculty accept AI—for different reasons—a mixture of personal and cultural influences and how that acceptance can shape research imagination.

The componential theory of creativity (CTC) is a meta- theory describing the social and psychological factors driving creativ- ity within an organisation. This theory explains the influence of the at- home and workplace on employees' creative actions (Amabile  [1983,](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) [2018)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for). The faculty defines Amabile's  ([2018)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) creativity theory research creativity as the capacity to generate innovative thoughts, create new projects and tackle challeng- ing problems in the academy. According to it, creativity arises from the interaction of three things: domain- specific knowl- edge (what is needed and skillful in the domain under study), cognition (the cognitive capacity leading to new thought) and motivation (the personal desire to act out of interest and plea- sure) (Amabile [2018)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for). AI could thus provide access to massive amounts of data and sophisticated analyses, thus contributing to faculty research creativity theory. Creative thinking has been positively influenced by technologies, for instance, as we employ them to analyse data, create new ideas and design novel research initiatives (Figoli, Mattioli, and Rampino [2022)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for).

The human- AI co- creation model describes the creativity process in the age of AI and how AI changes the playing field at each step. The model also looks at how AI can optimise each swoop of imaginative action and make the meaning more efficiently pre- sented. Its focus on co- design speaks to the importance of collab- oration and is an innovation in human- AI co- creation. Results from practical use examples indicate that AI creativity has influ- enced many fields, from opening new possibilities for individuals and society to opening new problems and possibilities in technol- ogy, society and education (Wu et al. 2021).

The creative empowerment approach emphasises harnessing technologies, especially AI, to help people and teams be cre- ative. AI is a creativity enabler, which could reduce bottlenecks and speed up data creation and analysis, opening up new pos- sibilities for creative ideas (Lee and Low 2024). The theory is that effective AI adoption and deployment can make a real dif- ference in faculty research imagination. With individual factors (intention and usefulness), environment (infrastructure and organisational infrastructure) and human–machine interaction in mind, this work shows the need for standardised tools to measure AI acceptance and to design for increased acceptance. Additionally, the system projects that AI will become more than a support technology; it will be a creative partner in research and learning.

**2.1 \| Summarising the Conceptualisation of Literature**

The rapid expansion of AI has changed the nature of research creativity, particularly among university faculty. Studying re- lated theoretical frameworks gives us a mixed picture of the relationship between AI adoption and research creativity. TAM focuses on ‘perceived usefulness’ and ‘perceived ease of use’ as primary drivers of technological adoption, driving attitudes and indirectly driving intentions to use AI in research. This is fol- lowed up by TPB, which consists of ‘attitude’, ‘subjective norms’ and ‘perceived behavioural control’, focussing on faculty percep- tions, social support and self- efficacy for AI use. UTAUT adds to this framework by treating ‘performance expectancy’, ‘effort ex- pectancy’, ‘social influence’ and ‘facilitating conditions’ as driv- ers of behaviour intention, which include personal motivation, cultural norms and institutional setting.

From the creativity angle, CTC focuses on domain expertise, thinking and motivation and suggests that AI will boost research creativity through access to big data and advanced analytics. In the human- AI co- creation model, AI optimally facilitates the entire creative cycle, making it possible to collaborate and cre- ate. The creative empowerment approach uses AI to lift the bar and accelerate ideation by simplifying data creation and analy- sis. Combined, such theories give us an integrative picture: AI helps but also works more closely with scientists, changing hab- its and reinventing possibilities. Such a synthesis calls for stan- dardised measures to evaluate AI acceptance and techniques to utilise fully in the lab and learning lab.

**3 \| Materials and Methods**

**3.1 \| Study Design**

The present research was a mixed- method study conducted from January 2024 to August 2024. The main aim of this study was to develop and evaluate the psychometric properties of AIA&RCS among Arab faculty members from Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. Due to their technological advancements and substantial invest- ments in the AI sector, these countries provide suitable aca- demic environments for examining the adoption of AI and its use in research creativity. To provide a clear methodological 

perspective, qualitative and quantitative phases are presented separately.

**3.3 \| Phase 2: Quantitative Phase**

**3.3.1 \| Participants**

Participants included Arab faculty members from Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. The in- clusion criteria included (a) having at least one year of faculty experience, (b) using AI tools in research and (c) having at least one published article in the context of creativity. Exclusion cri- teria included (a) answering more than 25% of items and (b) an- swering suspiciously, such as answering in random order or very fast (completing the survey in \< 5 min). For sample size estima- tion at 80% power, a criterion of 5–25 participants per item was used. Therefore, 720 faculty members were considered the final sample size.

For sample size estimation at 80% power, a criterion of 5–25 par- ticipants per item was used. Of the 720 faculty members who completed the survey, 439 participants (60.9%) were male, and 281 (39.1%) were female. The average age of the participants was 46.85 years (SD = 7.75), with an age range of 33 to 64 years. Additionally, the average years of professional experience was 

9.71 years (SD = 4.83), ranging from 5 to 23 years.

**3.3.2** \| **Procedures**

First, we searched systematically for faculty members at univer- sities in Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates who had at least one article published in Arabic or English on creativity. A list of these people, along with their email addresses, was drawn up. We then sent an email outlining the purpose of the study, how to participate, the protection of pri- vacy, and a brief description of the study. A Google Forms- based 

version of the AIA&RCS was developed online for access. The informed consent form was embedded on the first page of the retrieved URL. Participants were encouraged to review this form carefully. If they willingly consented, they were told to continue with the experiment; if not, they were told to withdraw the link.

**3.3.3** \| **Statical Analysis**

The SPSS 26 for EFA and AMOS 24 for CFA were used for data analysis. Further EGA was conducted using R- Studio software to supplement the validation.

Face validity was validated by qualitative and quantitative meth- ods to ensure the tool's reliability and veracity. For the qualita- tive assessment, ten of the target group members reviewed the scale and gave suggestions on the tool's usability, accuracy and layout. Their suggestions were carefully incorporated into the final draft. Quantitatively, all items whose scores fell below the cutoff of 1.5 were excluded so that only items that met the pre- defined relevance threshold were retained (Johnson 2021).

A group of 10 subject- matter experts tested content validity with decades of experience in quality research, tool development and online learning. These professionals scrutinised the instru- ment for fluency, grammatical correctness, item order and con- sistency. The content validity ratio (CVR) and content validity index (CVI) were calculated for this analysis. Items with a CVR above 0.62 and CVI above 0.79 were judged valid and retained to follow accepted validation guidelines (Almanasreh, Moles, and Chen [2019;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Binti Hassan [2018)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for).

EFA and CFA assessed the construct validity. The data were ran- domly assigned to two subgroups in a descriptive cross- sectional study of 360 people. The principal axis factoring (PAF) with Promax rotation performed EFA to detect clusters of highly cor- related variables. Tests to be tested initially included the Kaiser– Meyer–Olkin (KMO) test for sampling adequacy (if it was more significant than 0.60, it was suitable) and Bartlett's test of sphe- ricity (to ensure the existence of significant correlations in the data \[_p_ \< 0.05\]) (De Winter and Dodou [2012;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Hill 2011; Zhang et al. 2024; Kordbagheri, Abdelrahman, et al. 2024).

The maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) for CFA was con- ducted with AMOS 24 software. This step was to try out the proposed factor structure described in the EFA. We measured model fit using the root- mean- square error of approximation (RMSEA \< 0.08), comparative fit index (CFI \> 0.90), incremen- tal fit index (IFI \> 0.90), goodness- of- fit index (GFI \> 0.90) and Tucker- Lewis index (TLI \> 0.90) (Cheung and Rensvold [2002;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Marsh, Balla, and Hau  2013; Van Laar and Braeken  2021; Kordbagheri, Kordbagheri, et al. 2024). These indices provided a strong indication of the tool's structural integrity. Furthermore, multigroup analysis was used to test the four- factor structure for invariance based on gender and work experience: fit indices that changed below 0.1 indicate invariance (Kenny, Kaniskan, and McCoach 2015; Rajaeiramsheh et al. 2021). Convergent validity was assessed using AVE and CR as individual variables. AVE values \> 0.5 and CR values exceeding 0.7 were considered ac- ceptable, indicating the internal consistency and coherence of the model (dos Santos and Cirillo [2023)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for). Reliability analysis was 

also performed to verify internal consistency, and Cronbach's alpha above 0.70 assured the constructs' reliability (Chin and Yao [2021)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for).

**4 \| Results**

Based on the findings from interviews with faculty members, literature reviews and tools related to AI, the pool of items in- cluded 82 items (32 items derived from the literature review and 50 items from the qualitative section) in a 5- point Likert scale, ranging from strongly disagree to strongly agree. After several rounds of review by the research team, 40 items were either de- leted or merged, and the remaining 42 items were carried for- ward to the psychometric evaluation phase. During the face validity and content validity stages, no items were removed.

**4.1 \| Exploratory Factor Analysis**

To assess the adequacy of the sample size, the KMO test was used. The results showed that the sample size was adequate for factor analysis (KMO = 0.859). Additionally, Bartlett's test of sphericity indicated that the correlations between variables were sufficiently large and significant, making them appropri- ate for CFA (Chi- Square = 9672.39, df = 861, _p_ \< 0.000).

In the factor structure analysis of AIA&RCS, four factors with eigenvalues greater than one were identified, which were con- firmed by the scree plot. Furthermore, parallel analysis was used to verify the extracted factors, and the results indicated that the actual eigenvalues for four factors were significantly higher than the random eigenvalues. Therefore, both real and simulated analyses clearly identified four factors for AIA&RCS (Figure 1).

According to the Promax rotation, the four factors together explained 51.6% of the AIA&RCS variance. Factor 1, ‘Feeling of AI's Usefulness and Effectiveness in Research Creativity’, was the strongest, contributing 16.3% of the variance (ei- genvalue = 6.84), which suggests that we strongly think 

**FIGURE 1** \| Comparison of eigenvalues for real and random data in parallel analysis.

that AI contributes to research creativity. Factor 2, ‘Ethical Issues in Research’, contributed 12.4% of the variance (eigen- value = 5.19), indicating the ethical issues in the use of AI in research. Factor 3, ‘Respect of AI Powers’ explained 11.6% variance (eigenvalue = 4.87), so we can see that researchers are largely confident in AI's capacity to facilitate and improve research work. Lastly, Factor 4, “Regret to Use AI,” explained 11.4% of the variance (eigenvalue = 4.77), which indicates that researchers have a very positive interest in using AI technolo- gies in their future research projects.

The analysis also identified 10 items as dropped from the fac- tor table because their factor loading was \< 0.4, indicating weak relationships with factors. These included items: 24, 26, 27,29, 31,33, 34, 36, 38, 39 from ‘perceived AI effectiveness in research creativity’; 9, 10 and 12 from ‘ethical challenges in research’; 3 and 4 from ‘trust in AI capabilities’; and 20 and 21 from ‘willing- ness to use AI’ (Table 2).

Table 2 gave a complete summary of the EFA of the AIA&RCS showing the internal consistency of each element, factor load- ings, communities (_h_2) and eigenvalues for each factor to give an overall picture of the dimensionality of AI research constructs. These results had a lot to say about how AI was thought of and deployed in research, including the importance of perceived utility, ethical issues, trust and willingness among researchers to use AI tools. The enhanced factor structure facilitated re- searchers and practitioners to pinpoint the drivers of AI adop- tion in research for personalised intervention and improved AI- enabled research.

**4.2 \| Confirmatory Factor Analysis**

The goodness- of- fit indices from the CFA for the first- order four- factor model indicated that it was well- fitted, which is to say that it adequately captured the data structure. In par- ticular, CFA data indicated that RMSEA was below 0.08, a good model fit. In addition, the CFI, IFI, GFI and TLI were all above 0.90 which showed that the model is both valid and fitting. The factor loadings for items of the four factors in the first- order CFA model showed that 25 items of the AIA&RCS have factor loadings over 0.40 and are strongly associated with their factor. Not only that, but these loadings were also statistically significant at 0.001, implying strong connections between the items and latent factors. The results are therefore consistent with the AIA&RCS capturing im- portant aspects of AI- related research activities and attitudes among faculty (Table 3, Figure 2).

The first- order CFA fit indices of the four- factor AIA&RCS are shown in Table 3. The _Χ_2/df ratio of 3.03 is within the norms which confirms the model fit. Furthermore, the RMSEA of 0.075 is a good approximation of the covariance of the popu- lation, where the value of RMSEA is typically considered good for under 0.08. TLI, GFI, IFI and CFI were 0.928, 0.907, 0.936 and 0.936, respectively, all above 0.90 which is widely accepted as a measure of a well- fitting model. Such fit indices and large factor loadings indicate that AIA&RCS is indeed an appropri- ate and robust measure of AI research constructs. The fit of the model and the statistical significance of the factor loadings provide confirmation of factor strength and provide trust in the tool's ability to evaluate perceptions and behaviours around AI research use by faculty. Not only do the results contribute to the broader picture of how AI can be used in research but they also make us add more pieces to the literature on the application of AI technologies in higher education and research.

**4.3 \| Reliability**

The results showed that the internal consistency of AIA&RCS and its four factors, based on Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega, had values higher than 0.70. These results indicate an acceptable internal consistency for AIA&RCS. Additionally, the test–retest reliability results showed that between the ini- tial and follow- up times, AIA&RCS (_r_ = 0.89, _p_ \< 0.001) and its factors, perceived usefulness and effectiveness of AI in research creativity (_r_ = 0.92, _p_ \< 0.001), ethical challenges in research (_r_ = 0.84, _p_ \< 0.001), trust in AI capabilities (_r_ = 0.88, _p_ \< 0.001), and willingness to use AI (_r_ = 0.93, _p_ \< 0.001), showed satisfactory to strong temporal stability. Therefore, the results indicate that AIA&RCS has an acceptable stability reliability (Table 4).

**4.4 \| Convergent Validity**

The results showed that AVE and CR for the four factors of the AIA&RCS were above recommended levels of 0.50 and 0.70, re- spectively. For each criterion, the CRs for perceived usefulness and effectiveness of AI in research creativity (0.94), ethical challenges in research (0.95), trust in AI capabilities (0.93) and willingness to use AI (0.94) were much higher than their AVEs (0.66, 0.74, 0.73 and 0.76, respectively). Also, internal consis- tency indexes were equally high for all the variables—0.890 to 0.948 for Cronbach's alpha (), 0.845 to 0.948 for Cronbach's omega (). These findings show that the AIA&RCS is at least

**4.5 \| Analysis of Measurement Invariance Based on Gender and Years of Experience**

The results indicate a lack of measurement invariance for the six- factor model of AIA&RCS across the two subgroups of gen- der and years of experience. The absolute changes in CFI and RMSEA for the metric and scalar models compared to the refer- ence model were \< 0.1 (Table 5).

**4.6 \| Exploratory Graph Analysis**

The results of the EGA confirmed the four- factor structure of the AIA&RCS. All dimensions and items identified in the EGA were consistent with the findings from the EFA (Figure 3). The bootstrap EGA (bootEGA) employing 1000 bootstrap samples on the dataset indicates a median dimensionality of 4, suggesting that, on average, four dimensions form the identified commu- nities within the network. According to the frequency analysis, in 99.8% of the 1000 bootstrapped samples, a four- dimensional structure was observed. This configuration was observed 998 times, indicating that the four- dimensional solution appears to be more stable and dominant across the bootstrapped samples.

The results indicate that the values of structural consistency and stability for all items are above 0.75, which reflects adequate stability. Therefore, the identified four- dimensional structure is quite robust (Figure 3).

The AIA&RCS consists of 25 items and 4 dimensions. The three dimensions—‘trust in AI capabilities’, ‘ethical challenges in research’ and ‘willingness to use AI’—are related to the accep- tance of AI in research, while the dimension ‘perceived useful- ness and effectiveness of AI in research creativity’ pertains to the use of AI in research creativity. Scoring is based on a five- point Likert scale: strongly disagree (1), disagree (2), neutral (3), agree 

4. and strongly agree (5). It is important to note that all items in the dimensions ‘trust in AI capabilities’ and ‘ethical challenges in research’ are reverse scored. For the three dimensions related to AI acceptance in research, the score range is between 25 and 

<div></div>

125. A score lower than 50 indicates low acceptance, a score between 50 and 90 represents moderate acceptance and a score above 90 indicates high acceptance of AI in research. In the ‘per- ceived usefulness and effectiveness of AI in research creativity’ dimension (11 items), the minimum score is 11, and the maxi- mum score is 55. A score below 25 indicates low effectiveness, a score between 25 and 40 reflects moderate effectiveness and a score above 40 represents high effectiveness.

The study developed and validated the AIA&RCS among faculty members, identifying a four- factor structure: ‘perceived useful- ness and effectiveness of AI in research creativity’, ‘ethical chal- lenges in research’, ‘trust in AI capabilities’ and ‘willingness to use AI’. does not directly show up in the identified factors in this re- search, it is still part of the ‘trust in AI capabilities’ factor. Yet, this article adds ‘ethical problems in research’ and ‘frustra- tion with AI power’, which are ignored in previous models. Inclusion of ‘ethical challenges in research’ highlights con- cerns regarding the ethical issues around AI in academia, from data privacy to algorithmic bias to artificial substitution of human judgement. These findings agree with recent work on how we need to think about ethics in AI adoption (Jobin, Ienca, and Vayena 2019).

As the outcome of the present study ‘willingness to use AI’ matches ‘behavioural intention’ in TPB (Ajzen [1991)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for). If faculty feel positive about AI (e.g., ‘perceived usefulness and effective- ness of AI in research creativity’ and ‘trust in AI capabilities’), then it may encourage them to deploy the technology. ‘ethical challenges in research’ can also affect ‘subjective norms’, that is, ethical questions could impact the attitudes and social norms for the AI use (Wang et al. 2024).

Here, ‘perceived usefulness and effectiveness of AI’ compared to ‘performance expectancy’ of the UTAUT (Venkatesh et al. 2003). This indicates that faculty find AI a way to build their own exper- tise and create creative processes. ‘Loyalty in AI strengths’ can even impact internal motivation. If a user believes in the power of AI, then he is more likely to feel encouraged to apply it in his research. Also ‘ethical challenges in research’ are based on the policy- related and organisational norms environmental factors that can hinder research innovation. Such findings align with the elements of the integrated creativity theory (Amabile [2018)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for). Human- AI co- creation: A human- AI collaboration in creative tasks (Wu et al. 2021). As per the current outcome, the dimen- sions ‘aptitude of AI to be useful and effective’ and ‘truth in AI capabilities’ indicate cooperation. Creativity empowerment model (Lee and Low 2024): AI can help you think creatively on your own and as part of your team. The ‘perceived usefulness and effectiveness of AI’ variable shows that professors think about AI as a device to open the gates and allow creativity.

This study had higher than 0.9 Cronbach's alpha for both the whole scale and subscales, which shows very good inter- nal consistency. Typically, Cronbach's alpha above 0.7 shows good reliability and above 0.8 indicates a tool is good reli- ability (DeVellis and Thorpe  [2021)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for). Test–retest reliability: to evaluate the time- integrity of AIA&RCS, we applied the test– retest method. These intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) of the whole scale and subscales were between 0.84 and 0.93. Cicchetti ([1994)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) stated that, when ICC is between 0.75 and 0.85, this means that it is good; when it is above 0.85, then it is excel- lent (Cicchetti [1994)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for). Straub, Boudreau, and Gefen (2004) noted that ICC values \> 0.8 mean high reliability, and tools with this kind of stability can be applied to longitudinal studies and con- tinuous analyses (Straub, Boudreau, and Gefen 2004). These results are in line with other work from the world of psycho- metric tool development. For example, Teo and Noyes (2011) found that ICC values for testing technology acceptance mea- surement tools were similar which suggested good test–re- test reliability (Teo and Noyes 2011). Venkatesh et al. (2003) pointed out the importance of measurement tool reliability in their model and found high reliability predictive of intent and actions of technology use (Venkatesh et al. 2003). In addi- tion, in Teo and Noyes (2011), high reliability of attitudes- to- technology tools was presented as a fundamental determinant of education research (Teo and Noyes 2011).

In this research, the AIA&RCS achieved good convergent valid- ity as per Fornell and Larcker ([1981)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for). In the TAM, convergent validity is mentioned as a measurement device for technologies- acceptance constructs (Davis  [1989)](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for). The UTAUT model also includes convergent validity as a metric in the evaluation of mea- surement instruments (Venkatesh et al. 2003).

The EGA results confirmed the AIA&RCS four- factor structure, where each item was placed in the right factor. This result shows that the factor structure of the scale is stable and stable. EGA is a new method in psychometrics that makes use of graph theory to detect patterns in multivariate data. What is unique about EGA 

compared to the traditional factor analysis techniques is that it can uncover interesting and unexpected patterns within the data (Golino and Demetriou 2017).

These invariance tests revealed that the AIA&RCS were robust in both configural invariance and metric invariance, that is, items' factor structure and factor loadings were consistent between de- mographic subgroups (gender and years of experience). But in the current study, we found only partial difference in fixed values between subgroups in scalar invariance. Such shifts could be ex- plained by demographic differences based on perceptions and ac- tual use cases of AI. This research aligns with the TAM, TPB and UTAUT models, where key predictors of technology adoption are ‘perceived usefulness’ and ‘behavioural intention’ which tend to be the same for most demographic categories (Ajzen  [1991;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Davis [1989;](#conflicts-of-interest-cicchetti-d-v-1994-guidelines-criteria-and-rules-of-thumb-for) Venkatesh et al. 2003).

**6 \| Conclusion**

The 25- item AIA&RCS has proven to be a valid and useful way to determine whether faculty values and uses AI in an experi- mentational creative way. The scale's correct AVE and CR values mean that its items and factors measure precisely the theoretical objects intended. Furthermore, the EFA and CFA results also verify that the AIA&RCS is stable and robust in factor structure, making it more apprehensible in academic and research environ- ments. The EGA further confirmed that the tool was reliable and stable, making it easy for the researcher and educational admin- istrators to deploy it.

**6.1 \| Limitations and Future Direction**

This research reveals a wealth of information on the creation and validation of the 25- item AIA&RCS as a measure of AI acceptance and research creativity. Yet, there are some limitations to consider that might limit the interpretation and generalisation of the results.

The first was that they had faculty members working at uni- versities in specific areas—say, from certain Middle Eastern countries, Jordan and Saudi Arabia. This demographic circum- scription might hinder the application of the results to other regions or cultures. Extending the study to faculty from more countries and institutions might make the tool more universal. Second, the cross- sectional design is only an ebb and flow of views and actions, so the temporal effects of AI acceptance and its impact on research innovation are still to be discovered. A longitudinal study would be more informative in showing how these are changing over time.

The research was also based on self- reports, which could be bi- ased by social attractiveness or memory biases. Future studies might also include observational or experimental techniques to validate and supplement self- reports. And that was all quantita- tive analysis; adding qualitative approaches might help us un- derstand contextual and subjective aspects of AI adoption and its influence on research imagination.

To push the field, we might in the future ask how contex- tual factors (institutional policies, technology infrastructure, 

disciplinary differences) regulate the balance between AI ac- ceptance and research creativity. It might also look at the demo- graphic role of age, gender and academic standing in AI beliefs. Additionally, the ethics and practical difficulties of bringing AI to academic practice are important as they influence whether such technologies will ever be accepted and implemented broadly.

And last but not least, the study of the relationship between AI- driven tools and cross- disciplinary cooperation might provide an unusual window into how AI fosters innovation in different research areas. As we work through these limitations and along these directions, further studies could build on the AIA&RCS's application to be more robust and applicable to a range of aca- demic and research environments.

**6.2 \| Practical Implications**

This research has practical lessons for universities and policy- makers seeking to bring AI into research communities. With the AIA&RCS, institutions can measure faculty interest in AI and plan interventions (trainers, infrastructure) to promote adop- tion. Knowledge of moral issues, confidence and usefulness can then inform policies to overcome challenges such as data privacy and algorithmic bias and build a society of ethical AI use. In addition, the scale can be used to detect demographic or disciplinary differences in AI acceptance for personalised inter- ventions to encourage the human–AI interaction and research creativity across different academic environments.

## Ethics Statement The present study abstains from divulging confidential data, conducting experimentation or handling sensitive information, thereby obviating the necessity for publication consent. Ethical considerations were meticu- lously woven into the fabric of the research process, underscoring the im- peratives of participant autonomy, privacy and confidentiality. Measures were diligently implemented to uphold participant autonomy, ensuring the sanctity of their privacy and confidentiality, alongside furnishing exhaus- tive information elucidating the research's purpose. These ethical bench- marks were rigorously adhered to, preserving the study's integrity and reliability. Furthermore, recognising the absence of experimental protocols or sensitive data in our research, our university discerned the prudence in delineating ethical codes tailored explicitly for experimental inquiries. This initiative underscores our commitment to fostering ethically sound research practices, thereby fortifying the ethical underpinnings of future research endeavours. Also, all methods were carried out following relevant guidelines and regulations or the Declaration of Helsinki 1964.

**Consent** Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants in- cluded in the study.
